The '''OFDM-based Joint Communication and Sensing (JCAS) project''' develops a GNU Radio system in which one OFDM waveform carries data and provides channel measurements for sensing. The intended application is a quasi-bistatic automotive scenario with a transmitting and sensing node and a separate communication receiver.

== SDR hierarchy ==

* Parent page: [[Software Defined Radio (SDR)|Software Defined Radio (SDR)]]
* Hardware: [[NI USRP-2954R|NI USRP-2954R]]
* Current project page: '''OFDM-based Joint Communication and Sensing (JCAS)'''

__TOC__

== Project scope and status ==

The project covers an OFDM communication link, channel-response processing for sensing, and deployment on the [[NI USRP-2954R]]. The current repository contains a reproducible channel-model simulation. Hardware adaptation and quantitative sensing validation remain separate development tasks.

== Intended system architecture ==

The planned primary node uses one UBX-160 daughterboard for transmission and the other for sensing reception. The transmitted OFDM waveform is intended to serve two paths: a direct communication path to a separate communication receiver and a propagation path in which a target reflection is captured by the sensing receiver and processed into channel-frequency, channel-impulse, and delay-Doppler information. A second USRP acts as the communication receiver; its exact hardware configuration is not defined in the current repository. Both daughterboards on the primary USRP have been checked in transmit and receive configurations. Their final roles should be assigned only after comparable measurements have been recorded.

The main repository flowgraph does not yet implement this complete hardware diagram. It connects the transmitter to a software channel model and then to one receiver; there are no UHD Source or UHD Sink blocks in that graph.

== Recorded hardware results ==

The following is a concise record of the completed hardware checks. Test 1 stream counts refer to active TX and RX streams, not to daughterboard names. Test 2A and Test 2B use the project measurements near 5.8 GHz, with a 200 MHz master clock, 100 MS/s application rate, the same RF cable, and the recorded <code>Unknown PPS</code> synchronisation setting. Displayed Frequency Sink levels are dBFS; dBm values below refer to an instrument or input reference and are not interchangeable with display levels.

The trial set also requested 40 MS/s. The report records the matrix above rather than a separate 40 MS/s result. The 200 MS/s master clock permits integer-divisor rates such as 200, 100, and approximately 66.6 MS/s; Ethernet throughput and host processing limit the number of active streams. The report attributes the transmission-chain underflows at higher rates to host/GNU Radio processing and notes that real-time scheduling, code optimisation, or a more allocation-aware implementation may help. Both Ethernet links performed similarly; when one link was sufficient, the first USRP address was used as the default. A direct same-USRP TX-to-RX shortcut was affected by LO leakage at the receiver, while external instrumentation did not show that synchronisation-related problem.

=== Test 2A: transmitter measurements ===

The time-synchronisation check reported an offset of no more than 50 Hz for nearly all network synchronisation algorithms. GPS was the exception and may have been affected by the external GPS receiver; internet connectivity improved the observed performance.

The measured 5.8 GHz LO/image results were:

The report expects approximately -35 dB carrier suppression and -45 dB image rejection at a lower operating frequency. The harmonic result table reports 1.73 dBm fundamental and -51.73 dB second-harmonic distortion for its first row, and 1.56 dBm and -52.07 dB for its second row; both third harmonics were below the noise floor. The source result table labels those rows as daughterboards 0 and 1, so the raw numeric labels must not be inferred from an Ethernet port. The 1 kHz AM transmission with modulation index 0.7 was reported as matching the expected behaviour. Compression and saturation plots were recorded, but the report does not provide a numerical compression or saturation point.

=== Test 2B: receiver measurements ===

For the LO/image check, a -30 dBm CW tone was applied at 5.801 GHz and observed with a rectangular-window FFT of size 8192. The results were:

The receiver input limit is -15 dBm. In the compression test, a -22.58 dB attenuator was used. At both 20 dB and 37.5 dB RX gain, the generator range from -30 to -20 dBm was reported as irregular, likely because the tone was close to the noise floor and the FFT response was sensitive to small changes. With 20 dB gain, the response was linear from a -20 to 7 dBm generator setting, corresponding to -15 dBm at the receiver input with the recorded attenuator; compression or saturation was not reached. With 37.5 dB gain, the response was linear from -20 to 0 dBm and unstable from 0 to 5 dBm. These observations identify the tested operating region; they are not a standardized P1dB result.

The IIP3 tests used +2 and +3 MHz tones; the IIP2 tests used +2 and +5 MHz tones. In both tests, the tones were generated through the other daughterboard with amplitude 0.5 and TX gain 0, at the 5.8 GHz tune, 100 MS/s, and 37.5 dB RX gain. The intercept calculations use the documented dBFS differences, while only the input reference is absolute dBm. The reported IIP2 values are well above the tested receiver-input limit; the result report therefore expects this second-order nonlinearity not to affect the planned experiments. The values are measurement results under the recorded setup, not universal specifications for every gain, bandwidth, connector, or frequency.

== Why OFDM can support both functions ==

OFDM divides the occupied bandwidth among orthogonal subcarriers. Data symbols are transmitted in parallel, while known preambles and pilots support synchronisation and channel estimation. A cyclic prefix copies the end of each OFDM symbol to its beginning, which reduces inter-symbol interference when it is longer than the relevant channel delay spread.

For communication, the receiver estimates the channel, equalises the data carriers, and decodes the payload. For sensing, the same received frame is compared with an estimate of the transmitted subcarrier symbols. Variation across subcarriers represents delay-dependent channel structure; variation across successive OFDM symbols represents Doppler-dependent structure. The two branches therefore reuse the same waveform, but they need different validation criteria.

== Current simulation signal chain ==

The reference launchers generate seven repetitions of the byte values 0 to 255, giving a 1792-byte payload. The tagged payload is modulated by the OFDM transmitter and passed through the simulated channel model before reaching the custom receiver. The receiver produces decoded bytes for the BER calculation and also exposes active-carrier samples for the CFR, CIR, and DDM processing. A Throttle block controls the software-only simulation. It must be removed when the graph is replaced by hardware sources or sinks.

=== OFDM frame ===

The transmitter uses a 128-point inverse FFT. Of the 128 bins, 127 are active: 115 carry header or payload data and 12 are pilots. The Nyquist bin is unused. The current pilot bins are -55, -45, -35, -25, -15, -5, 5, 15, 25, 35, 45, and 55, with pilot value 1.

Both header and payload use QPSK, and scrambling is disabled in the main flowgraph. The frame begins with two synchronisation words:

* the first is a Zadoff–Chu sequence placed on alternating active carriers, producing the repeated time-domain halves used by the synchroniser; and
* the second is a fixed-seed BPSK sequence used for channel estimation.

After the header and payload symbols are assigned to carriers, the transmitter performs the inverse FFT and adds the cyclic prefix.

=== Simulated channel ===

<code>Flow_graphs/Channel_Model.grc</code> adds three copies of the signal and complex Gaussian noise. The direct copy has zero delay and scale factor 1. The other copies are delayed by 20 and 40 samples, scaled by 0.2, and multiplied by 200 Hz and 100 Hz complex sources respectively. Those sources have amplitudes 0.3 and 0.2. The Gaussian-noise amplitude is 0.001.

These values are diagnostic simulation settings, not a calibrated vehicular channel model. The channel hierarchy has its own fixed 100 kS/s rate parameter. A change to the top-level sample rate must therefore be checked against the channel hierarchy and its Doppler-source timing.

=== Receiver ===

The custom receiver has two inputs and three outputs.

{| class="wikitable"
! Port
! Stream
! Use in the main graph
|-
| Input 0
| Complex received samples
| Synchronisation, header recovery, payload recovery, and sensing-symbol extraction
|-
| Input 1
| Float frequency-correction control
| Connected to a constant zero in the current simulation, so the correction oscillator applies no fine-frequency adjustment
|-
| Output 0
| Decoded bytes
| Received-data display and PDU-based BER calculation
|-
| Output 1
| Serialised, unequalised active-carrier samples
| Received-symbol term in the CFR calculation; the main graph first scales it by <code>1/N</code>
|-
| Output 2
| Softly equalised active-carrier samples
| Estimate of the transmitted active-carrier symbols used in the CFR denominator
|}

The synchroniser uses the repeated halves of the first preamble and triggers on the falling edge of its correlation metric at a threshold of 0.996. A header/payload demultiplexer separates the frame. The two preambles initialise the channel estimate; the payload branch uses a decision-feedback equaliser with adaptation factor 0.1. The main graph currently leaves the external fine-frequency correction input at zero because applying the estimated correction caused unstable DDM behaviour in the assumed synchronised simulation.

=== Communication branch ===

The receiver reconstructs packed payload bytes. The BER block converts transmitted and received tagged streams to PDUs, matches them by the recovered <code>packet_num</code>, counts differing bits, and reports cumulative bit errors divided by cumulative compared bits.

This BER value describes only packets that reach the comparison block. Packet loss, acquisition failure, and unmatched packets need separate accounting in a complete link evaluation.

=== Sensing branch ===

For each active subcarrier <code>k</code> and OFDM symbol <code>m</code>, the graph forms a channel-frequency-response estimate of the form:

<pre>
H[k,m] = (Y[k,m] / N) / X_est[k,m]
</pre>

Here <code>Y</code> is the unequalised receiver output, <code>X_est</code> is the softly equalised estimate of the transmitted active-carrier symbol, and <code>N</code> is the configured number of active carriers. The samples are assembled column by column into an <code>N × M</code> matrix. A truncation block retains either all <code>M</code> symbols or the first <code>M-1</code>, according to <code>M_crop</code>.

{| class="wikitable"
! Product
! Current calculation
! Current display
|-
| Channel frequency response (CFR)
| Element-wise received/reference ratio on the active carriers
| Real part of the <code>N × M_crop</code> matrix
|-
| Channel impulse response (CIR)
| Orthonormal IFFT of the CFR along the subcarrier dimension
| Real part of the <code>N × M_crop</code> matrix
|-
| Delay-Doppler map (DDM)
| Configurable two-dimensional window, zero-padding, IFFT across subcarriers, FFT across symbols, then magnitude squared
| Linear magnitude-squared view and a view converted with <code>10 log10</code>
|}

The resolution factor controls zero-padding and display sampling; it does not improve the physical delay or Doppler resolution of the waveform. CFR and CIR windows show only the real component, not magnitude. The DDM values are processing outputs and are not calibrated received power, radar cross section, or detection probability.

The launchers do not pass a carrier frequency to the DDM visualisers. In that mode the horizontal increment is calculated as a simulated Doppler frequency, although the window still labels the axis as velocity in m/s. A physical velocity interpretation requires a non-zero carrier frequency and validation of the complete axis calculation.

By contrast, the initial hardware RF checks use a 200 MHz USRP master clock and request 100 MS/s. Always identify whether a number belongs to the launcher simulation, the raw GRC fields, or a hardware measurement.

== Running the simulation ==

The reference environment is GNU Radio 3.10.x; the repository records 3.10.12.0. Python, NumPy, SciPy, pyzmq, PyQt5, pyqtgraph, and SIP must be available in the same environment.

On Linux, clone the repository and run the reference launcher:

<pre>
git clone https://git.rwth-aachen.de/ihf/sdr/jcas-ofdm.git
cd jcas-ofdm

./Simulation_starter.sh --check
./Simulation_starter.sh
</pre>

Activate the intended Conda or Radioconda environment first if GNU Radio is not installed system-wide. <code>PYTHON_BIN</code> and <code>GRCC_BIN</code> can select explicit executables. On Windows, set the local Radioconda activation path near the start of <code>Simulation_starter.bat</code>, then run the batch file.

The Windows launcher compiles against the custom block definitions installed in its GNU Radio environment. Unlike the Linux launcher, it does not repair the legacy definitions in <code>Block_definition/</code> at launch time. Before relying on the Windows path, confirm that the installed transmitter and receiver definitions use the current class names and expose the receiver's complex-sample and float-correction inputs.

A normal run should show received data and BER in the GNU Radio window and open separate CFR, CIR, DDM dB, and DDM linear windows. Check for import, compilation, port-binding, vector-size, and flowgraph errors before interpreting the plots.

The plotters write binary diagnostic files under <code>Raw_data/</code>. They overwrite their respective file at startup and can grow during long runs. Use <code>--no-diagnostics</code> with the Linux launcher when those captures should be removed at shutdown.

== Hardware verification and development priorities ==

Detailed procedures and result records belong in <code>docs/First_tests.md</code>. At overview level, the sequence is:

# verify host connectivity and streaming;
# compare both transmitter RF chains;
# compare both receiver RF chains;
# verify the timing and frequency relationship needed between daughterboards;
# establish pure OFDM communication;
# validate sensing with a known static scene; and
# demonstrate joint communication and sensing over the air.

The most important next steps are to preserve complete measurement records, select the primary-USRP TX and sensing-RX roles from comparable data, connect a controlled UHD hardware path, verify synchronisation, and calibrate the sensing axes and levels against known delay and Doppler cases. Only then should static-target and joint over-the-air results be described as validated.

The committed custom-block definitions and generated main Python graph also need to be regenerated from, and aligned with, the current GRC and hand-written receiver. The Linux launcher works around the legacy definition names and missing float input in temporary files; that workaround should not be mistaken for source consistency.

Communication evaluation should distinguish BER on matched packets from acquisition failures and lost packets. Candidate measures include EVM, spectral efficiency, and peak-to-average power ratio. Sensing evaluation should cover measured delay and Doppler resolution, unambiguous regions, sidelobes, processing gain, and detection performance. These are evaluation goals; they are not all current program outputs.

== Interpretation limits ==

* A screen level is not absolute RF power unless the full path and display scaling have been calibrated.
* A simulated peak is not a detected target; the current graph has no detector or false-alarm control.
* Zero-padded bins make a plot smoother but do not create physical resolution.
* A successful communication decode does not prove that sensing timing, phase coherence, or axes are correct.
* Hardware sample rates and the reference simulation rate are different configurations and must not be mixed in a result.
* Every quantitative result should identify the code revision, waveform parameters, channel or RF setup, reference plane, normalisation, and known limitations.

== Continuing the project ==

Start with <code>README.md</code> for orientation, then read <code>MAINTENANCE.md</code>, the main GRC files, <code>OFDMJCAStxrx.py</code>, and the current test document. Work on a focused branch, run the Linux preflight or the corresponding Windows checks, and compare the observed frame sizes and peaks with the configured channel before opening a merge request.

When the implementation changes, update the source-of-truth file first. Keep block definitions, stream signatures, coupled parameters, launcher defaults, plot vector sizes, ports, and documentation consistent. Do not commit generated captures, local environment paths, or Python caches.
